source_text: Διὰ δὴ τοῦτο οὐχ ἁπλῶς εἶπεν, Ὕπαγε, πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα, ἵνα μὴ νόμον εἶναι νομίσῃς τὸ λεγόμενον, ἀλλὰ πῶς; Εἰ ἐθέλεις τέλειος εἶναι, ὕπαγε, πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα· ἵνα μάθῃς ὅτι ἐν τῇ γνώμῃ τῶν ἀκουόντων τὸ πρᾶγμα κεῖται. Ὅτι μὲν οὖν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις ταῦτα ἐπετέτακτο μόνοις, δῆλον ἐντεῦθεν· ἀλλ' οὐδέπω τὴν λύσιν εὑρήκαμεν. Εἰ γὰρ καὶ αὐτοῖς τοῦτο νενομοθέτηται μόνοις, τίνος ἕνεκεν ἐπιταγέντες μηδὲ ὑποδήματα ἔχειν, μηδὲ διπλοῦν ἱμάτιον, εὑρίσκονται, ὁ μὲν σανδάλια κεκτημένος, ὁ δὲ καὶ φελόνην ἔχων; Τί οὖν ἂν εἴποιμεν πρὸς ταῦτα; Ὅτι οὔτε αὐτοὺς μέχρι παντὸς ἀφῆκεν ὑπὸ ταύτην εἶναι τῶν νόμων τὴν ἀνάγκην, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τὸν σωτήριον ἰέναι μέλλων θάνατον, ἀπέλυσεν αὐτοὺς τῆς νομοθεσίας ταύτης. Πόθεν τοῦτο δῆλον; Ἀπ' αὐτῶν τῶν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ῥημάτων. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἔμελλεν ἐπὶ τὸ πάθος ὁδεύειν, καλέσας αὐτούς φησιν· Ὅτε ἀπέστειλα ὑμᾶς ἄτερ βαλαντίου καὶ πήρας, μή τινος ὑστερήσατε; Οἱ δὲ ἀποκριθέντες εἶπον· Οὐδενός. Ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Ἀλλὰ νῦν ὁ ἔχων βαλάντιον, ἀράτω, καὶ πή ραν· καὶ ὁ μὴ ἔχων, πωλησάτω τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀγοράσει μάχαιραν. Ἀλλ' ἴσως εἴποι τις ἂν, ὅτι Τοὺς μὲν ἀποστόλους διὰ τῶν εἰρημένων ἀπήλλαξας τῶν ἐγκλημάτων· τὸ δὲ ζητούμενόν ἐστιν εἰπεῖν, τίνος ἕνεκεν ἐναντία ὁ Χριστὸς ἐνομοθέτησε, ποτὲ μὲν λέγων, Μὴ κτήσησθε πήραν, ποτὲ δὲ λέγων, Ὁ ἔχων βαλάντιον, ἀράτω, καὶ πήραν. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν τοῦτο πεποίηκεν; Ἀξίως τῆς αὐτοῦ σοφίας καὶ προνοίας τῆς ὑπὲρ τῶν μαθητῶν. Παρὰ μὲν γὰρ τὴν ἀρχὴν ταῦτα ἐπέταξεν, ἵνα ἔργῳ καὶ πείρᾳ τὴν ἀπόδειξιν τῆς αὐτοῦ δυνάμεως λάβωσι, καὶ λαβόντες θαῤῥήσωσι λοιπὸν εἰς τὴν οἰκουμένην ἐξελθεῖν ἅπασαν. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ λοιπὸν ἱκανῶς ἔγνωσαν αὐτοῦ τὴν δύναμιν, ἐβούλετο καὶ αὐτοὺς οἴκοθεν τὴν αὐτῶν ἀρετὴν ἐπιδείξασθαι, καὶ μὴ μέχρι τέλους αὐτοὺς διαβαστάζεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἐνδιδόναι πολλαχοῦ καὶ συγχωρεῖν, καὶ πειρασμοὺς αὐτοὺς ὑπομένειν, ἵνα μὴ διὰ τέλους ἀργοὶ μένωσι. Καὶ καθάπερ οἱ νήχεσθαι διδάσκοντες, παρὰ μὲν τὰς ἀρχὰς τὰς αὐτῶν ὑποτιθέντες χεῖρας μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς ἀκριβείας τοὺς μαθητὰς τοὺς ἑαυτῶν διαβαστάζουσι, μετὰ δὲ πρώτην καὶ δευτέραν καὶ τρίτην ἡμέραν πολλαχοῦ τὴν δεξιὰν αὐτῶν ὑποσύραντες ἐκείνοις, κελεύουσιν ἑαυτοῖς βοηθεῖν, καί που καὶ μικρὸν βαπτίζεσθαι ἐπιτρέπουσι, καὶ πολλὴν τῷ στόματι δέχεσθαι τὴν ἅλμην· οὕτω δὴ καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἐποίησεν ἐπὶ τῶν μαθητῶν. Ἐν ἀρχῇ καὶ ἐν προοιμίοις οὐ μικρὸν, οὐ μέγα αὐτοὺς ἀφῆκε παθεῖν, ἀλλὰ πανταχοῦ παρῆν τειχίζων αὐτοὺς, περιφράττων, πάντα μετὰ ἀφθονίας αὐτοῖς ἐπιῤῥεῖν παρασκευάζων· ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἔδει καὶ τὴν ἀνδρείαν αὐτοὺς ἐπιδείξασθαι τὴν αὐτῶν, συνέστειλεν ὀλίγῳ τὴν χάριν, ἐγκελευσάμενος αὐτοῖς πολλὰ καὶ δι' ἑαυτῶν ἀνύειν. Διά τοι τοῦτο, ὅτε μὲν οὐκ εἶχον ὑποδήματα, οὐδὲ ζώνην, οὐδὲ ῥάβδον, οὐδὲ χαλκὸν, οὐδενὸς ὑστερήθησαν· Μή τινος γὰρ, φησὶν, ὑστερήσατε; Οἱ δὲ ἀποκριθέντες εἶπον· Οὐδενός. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ αὐτοὺς ἐκέλευσε καὶ βαλάντιον ἔχειν, καὶ πήραν, καὶ ὑποδήματα, εὑρίσκονται καὶ πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες καὶ γυμνητεύοντες. Ὅθεν δῆλον, ὅτι πολλαχοῦ συνεχώρει καὶ παρακινδυνεύειν αὐτοὺς καὶ στενοχωρεῖσθαι, ἵνα τινὰ μισθὸν ἔχωσιν Οὕτω που καὶ οἱ ὄρνιθες τοῖς νεοττοῖς ποιοῦσι τοῖς ἑαυτῶν· καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖνοι, ἕως μὲν τὰ πτερὰ ἁπαλὰ ἔχουσιν, ἐπὶ τῆς καλιᾶς καθήμενοι θάλπουσιν· ἐπειδὰν δὲ ἴδωσι πτεροφυήσαντας, καὶ δυναμένους τὸν ἀέρα τέμνειν, πρῶτον μὲν περὶ αὐτὴν τὴν καλιὰν ἵπτασθαι παρασκευάζουσιν, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ ποῤῥωτέρω περιάγουσι, παρὰ μὲν τὴν ἀρχὴν ἑπόμεναι καὶ διαβαστάζουσαι, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα αὐτοὺς ἑαυτοῖς ἀφιεῖσαι βοηθεῖν.
thought_title: Why Christ first forbade, then allowed possessions
orientation: Chrysostom is defending the apostles against the charge that they disobeyed Christ's command to possess nothing, and now explains why Christ later changed the command.
pass_a_gloss: For this very reason he did not simply say, Go, sell your possessions, so that you might not think the saying is a law, but how? If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions; so that you might learn that the matter lies in the judgment of the hearers. That therefore these things had been commanded to the apostles alone, is clear from this; but we have not yet found the solution. For if this has been legislated for them alone, for what reason, having been commanded to have not even sandals, nor a double cloak, are they found, one possessing sandals, and another also having a cloak? What then might we say to these things? That he did not leave them under this necessity of the laws until the end, but when he was about to go to the saving death, he released them from this legislation. From where is this clear? From the very words of the Savior. For since he was about to journey to the passion, having called them he says: When I sent you without purse and bag, did you lack anything? And they answered and said: Nothing. And he said to them: But now let the one who has a purse take it, and a bag; and the one who does not have, let him sell his cloak, and he will buy a sword. But perhaps someone might say, that You have freed the apostles from the charges through what has been said; but what is being sought is to say, for what reason Christ legislated contrary things, at one time saying, Do not acquire a bag, at another time saying, Let the one who has a purse take it, and a bag. For what reason then has he done this? Worthily of his wisdom and providence over the disciples. For at the beginning he commanded these things, so that by deed and by trial they might receive the demonstration of his power, and having received it they might be bold henceforth to go out into the whole inhabited world. But since they now knew his power sufficiently, he wished them also to display their own virtue from their own resources, and not to be carried by him until the end, but to give way in many places and to permit, and to endure trials, so that they might not remain idle through to the end. And just as those who teach swimming, at the beginnings placing their hands under them with much precision carry their own disciples, but after the first and second and third day in many places withdrawing their right hand from them, they command them to help themselves, and somewhere they also permit them to be dipped a little, and to take much brine into the mouth; so indeed also Christ did with the disciples. In the beginning and in the preludes he did not allow them to suffer anything small or great, but he was present everywhere walling them around, fencing them about, preparing all things to flow to them with abundance; but when it was necessary for them also to display their own courage, he contracted the grace a little, having exhorted them to accomplish many things also through themselves. For this very reason, when they did not have sandals, nor a belt, nor a staff, nor copper, they lacked nothing; For did you lack anything, he says? And they answered and said: Nothing. But when he commanded them also to have a purse, and a bag, and sandals, they are found both hungering and thirsting and going naked. From which it is clear, that in many places he permitted them both to run risks and to be distressed, so that they might have some reward. So somewhere also the birds do to their own chicks; for those also, as long as they have tender wings, sitting on the nest keep them warm; but when they see them fledged, and able to cut the air, first they prepare them to fly around the nest itself, then they lead them around farther, at the beginning following and carrying them, but after these things leaving them to help themselves.

choices.term: ἐν τῇ γνώμῃ τῶν ἀκουόντων τὸ πρᾶγμα κεῖται
choices.english: the matter lies in the judgment of the hearers
choices.why: γνώμη is the hearer's deliberate judgment or choice, matching the brief's 'disposition' sense; 'lies in' preserves κεῖται literally
rejected: the matter depends on the hearers' will
the thing is placed in the hearers' mind

choices.term: ἐπὶ τὸν σωτήριον ἰέναι μέλλων θάνατον
choices.english: when he was about to go to the saving death
choices.why: σωτήριον is adjectival 'saving' modifying θάνατον, not a separate noun; keeps the paradox of the saving death

choices.english: he released them from this legislation
choices.why: ἀπολύω with genitive means release from an obligation; 'legislation' keeps the legal frame Chrysostom has built
rejected: he freed them from this law
he dismissed them from this lawgiving

choices.why: the articular infinitive with διδάσκοντες is a standard Greek way to say 'swimming teachers'; keeps the image concrete

choices.english: they permit them to be dipped a little
choices.why: βαπτίζω here is literal dipping in water, not baptism; 'a little' keeps μικρόν adverbial
rejected: they allow them to be baptized a little

choices.english: he contracted the grace a little
choices.why: συστέλλω means to draw in or reduce; 'grace' is Chrysostom's term for divine help, and 'a little' keeps the dative of degree

pass_b_english: This is why he did not simply say, “Go, sell your possessions,” so that you would not think the saying was a law. How did he say it? “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions” (Matthew 19:21)—so that you might learn that the matter lies in the judgment of the hearers. Now, that these things had been commanded to the apostles alone is clear from this. But we have not yet found the solution. For even if this was legislated for them alone, why is it that although they were commanded to have no sandals and no second tunic, one of them is found owning sandals, and another even has a cloak? What then should we say to this? That he did not leave even them under the necessity of these laws forever, but when he was about to go to the saving death, he released them from this legislation. Where is this clear? From the Savior’s own words. For when he was about to journey to the passion, he called them and said, “When I sent you out without a purse or a bag, did you lack anything?” They answered, “Nothing.” Then he said to them, “But now let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who has none sell his cloak and buy a sword” (Luke 22:35-36).

But perhaps someone might say, “You have freed the apostles from the charges by what you have said, but the question remains: why did Christ legislate contrary things, at one time saying, ‘Do not acquire a bag’ (Matthew 10:9-10), and at another, ‘Let the one who has a purse take it, and a bag’?” Why then did he do this? In a manner worthy of his wisdom and his providence for his disciples. At the beginning he commanded these things so that by deed and experience they might receive the proof of his power, and having received it, might from then on have confidence to go out into the whole world. But once they had come to know his power sufficiently, he wanted them also to display their own virtue from within themselves, and not to be carried by him to the end, but himself to yield ground in many places and allow them to endure trials, so that they might not remain idle forever.

Just as those who teach swimming, at the beginning place their hands under their students and carry them with great care, but after the first, second, and third day they often withdraw their right hand from them and tell them to help themselves, and somewhere they even permit them to be dipped a little and to take in a great deal of salt water with their mouths—so Christ did with his disciples. At the beginning and in the first stages he did not allow them to suffer anything small or great, but he was present everywhere, walling them in, fencing them about, preparing everything to flow to them in abundance. But when they needed to display their own courage, he contracted the grace a little, urging them to accomplish many things by themselves.

For this reason, when they had no sandals, no belt, no staff, no copper coins, they lacked nothing. “Did you lack anything?” he says. They answered, “Nothing.” But when he commanded them to have a purse and a bag and sandals, they are found hungry and thirsty and going naked. From this it is clear that in many places he allowed them to face danger and be hard pressed, so that they might have some reward. This is something like what birds do with their young. As long as their wings are tender, they sit on the nest and keep them warm. But when they see that they have fledged and are able to cut the air, they first make them fly around the nest itself, then lead them farther out—at the beginning following and carrying them, but after that leaving them to help themselves.

last_rejected.quote: and another even has a cloak
last_rejected.why: Source says 'the one' (ὁ δὲ) has a cloak; English 'another' implies a different person from the sandals-owner, but Greek likely means the same Peter.
last_rejected.fix: and the one even has a cloak
last_rejected.ruling: ὁ δὲ means 'but the one/another,' standard adversative particle; 'another' is normal English rendering, not specific to Peter.

last_rejected.source_quote: Εἰ ἐθέλεις τέλειος εἶναι, ὕπαγε, πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα
last_rejected.why: The source quotes Christ's words to the rich young man, but this is not Matthew 19:21 in the source context. The source is discussing the apostles' mission instructions and their change, not the rich young man passage. The citation appears to be an editorial addition not supported by the source text, which is discussing Luke 22:35-36 and related mission commands.
last_rejected.fix: Remove the scripture reference or verify if this is a different passage being discussed.
last_rejected.ruling: The quote exactly matches Matt 19:21; the citation is a correct scripture reference, not a wrong one.

last_rejected.quote: to yield ground in many places
last_rejected.why: The Greek means 'to give way, yield, permit' not 'yield ground' as in retreating. It means Christ allowed/gave them permission in many places, not that they retreated.
last_rejected.fix: to give them permission in many places and allow them
last_rejected.ruling: ἐνδιδόναι πολλαχοῦ means 'give way in many places'; 'yield ground' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: γυμνητεύοντες means 'lacking a cloak/undergarment, poorly clothed' not completely naked. The disciples had cloaks they were told to sell for swords.
last_rejected.fix: poorly clothed or lacking proper garments
last_rejected.ruling: γυμνητεύοντες can mean 'going naked'; within normal range, not a changed meaning.

problems.quote: he wanted them also to display their own virtue from within themselves, and not to be carried by him to the end, but to yield ground in many places and allow them to endure trials
problems.source_quote: ἐβούλετο καὶ αὐτοὺς οἴκοθεν τὴν αὐτῶν ἀρετὴν ἐπιδείξασθαι, καὶ μὴ μέχρι τέλους αὐτοὺς διαβαστάζεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἐνδιδόναι πολλαχοῦ καὶ συγχωρεῖν, καὶ πειρασμοὺς αὐτοὺς ὑπομένειν
problems.why: The parallel infinitive makes 'them' the apparent subject of 'yield ground' and 'allow them,' obscuring that Christ is the one stepping back and permitting trials.
problems.fix: he wanted them also to display their own virtue from within themselves and not be carried to the end; rather, he chose to step back at times and allow them to endure trials
problems.ruling: ἐνδιδόναι καὶ συγχωρεῖν imply Christ yields; English chains 'them…to yield' and blurs who permits trials.

edits.old: he wanted them also to display their own virtue from within themselves, and not to be carried by him to the end, but to yield ground in many places and allow them to endure trials
edits.new: he wanted them also to display their own virtue from within themselves, and not to be carried by him to the end, but himself to yield ground in many places and allow them to endure trials

fixed: agency: fixed — Greek ἐνδιδόναι πολλαχοῦ καὶ συγχωρεῖν has Christ as subject, so inserted 'himself' to make Christ the one stepping back and permitting trials.

problems.why: Luke 10:4 uses “carry” (Μὴ βαστάζετε), not “acquire”; “Do not acquire” (Μὴ κτήσησθε) with “bag” (πήραν) comes from Matthew 10:9–10.
problems.ruling: Source quotes Μὴ κτήσησθε πήραν; Luke 10:4 says Μὴ βαστάζετε, so the citation misleads.

fixed: wrong_scripture: corrected citation to Matthew 10:9-10, since source Μὴ κτήσησθε πήραν matches Matthew 10:9-10, not Luke 10:4 (Μὴ βαστάζετε).
